title: Concentration Inequalities and Martingale Inequalities: A Survey
abstractRaw: We examine a number of generalized and extended versions of concentration inequalities and martingale inequalities. These inequalities are effective for analyzing processes with quite general conditions as illustrated in an example for an infinite Polya process and web graphs.

title: A decision support toolkit for AI-ready neuroscience data governance
authors: Wilhelmina M. Botes, Artur Mendes, Bart Huffman, Madison Fleischaker, Ciara Staunton, Beverley Townsend, Paul Ogendi, Lukman Abdulrauf, Andrea Parziale, Gabriela Skoczylas-Kizak
abstractRaw:
Contemporary human neuroscience relies on exchanging and analyzing neurodata across global institutions and
jurisdictions. However, regulatory architecture fails to maintain continuity of protection across distributed research
environments. Our comparison of 93 countries and 10 operative governance units across Africa, Europe, Latin
America and the Caribbean, and North America shows that neurodata are rarely recognized as distinct regulatory
objects, usually falling under broader legal classifications. While international sharing is permitted in principle,
transformation into derivatives, embeddings, and AI models raises questions about the scope and implementation of
continuing safeguards. We show that international exchange is defined by conditional interoperability, where effective
safeguards require aligning legal, institutional, and technical controls. To operationalize these findings, we introduce a
modular governance toolkit for the data-to-model lifecycle, including a Neurodata Risk Classification Framework,
decision support tools for neurodata transfer and transformation, and a Neurodata Transfer and Access Agreement to
sustain protection without global legal harmonization.

title: Audience engagement in live and recorded performance: a social liveness perspective
authors: Robin Ren, Joseph Devlin, John S. Hogan, Jorina von Zimmermann, Helen Nuttall, Daniel C. Richardson
abstractRaw: The best memories in life are often collective, from the roar of a stadium to the applause in a concert hall. The value of those moments can be seen in ratings of engagement, feelings of social affiliation, and synchronies in behaviour and autonomic arousal. But what exactly produces the value of the collective experience of a performance? Is it the presence of performers (physical liveness), the presence of other audience members (social liveness), or the fact they are sharing a stimulus? We looked at a range of collective experiences from live theatre to public cinemas to small group viewing in which we varied the two dimensions of liveness and tracked engagement through physiological synchrony. Our goal was to explore some of the many elements that contribute to liveness and engagement. We found that higher liveness, whether physical or social, fostered higher audience engagement and elevated heart rate synchrony. However, co-present pairs were not always more synchronised than pseudo-pairs who watched the same narrative stimuli at different times, suggesting that collective entrainment is not a uniform consequence of ‘being together’. We argue that while many dimensions of sociality might contribute to social liveness, understanding how they combine, how they are balanced with the narrative stimuli to foster collective entrainment without being distracted is the key to creating an engaging collective experience.

title: Can Chimpanzees Imagine a Blue Banana?
abstractRaw: Can a chimpanzee that has learned words for colors and objects find a blue pencil among pencils, straws, and Lego pieces in red, green, and blue? This seemingly simple task requires more than recognizing individual words: it requires integrating the meaning of a color adjective with that of a noun to identify an object possessing both properties. Children typically master this ability by 2.3 years. By age 3, they can integrate two modifiers, such as size and color, to follow instructions like “Find a large green straw.” These achievements mark important milestones in the development of language comprehension, allowing children to combine multiple words into a unified mental representation of an object. Chimpanzees, by contrast, can learn hundreds of words referring to objects, colors, and actions. Yet, despite decades of research, they have not been demonstrated to reliably integrate even a color with a noun. In this paper, we propose a simple neurocognitive account of adjective–noun comprehension. We argue that this ability depends on the development of neural connections that allow the prefrontal cortex to modify sensory representations of objects in posterior cortical regions. This framework offers a testable explanation for a fundamental difference between human and chimpanzee language comprehension.

title: I Remember That Question: Using Eye Tracking to See How Prequestions Shape Reading
abstractRaw:
Answering questions before learning (prequestions) improves memory for the information they
address, but how it does so is unclear. A common proposal is that prequestions direct attention to
that information. We tested this account by recording eye movements while participants read a
text about polio and tuberculosis after answering prequestions about one topic or none, so that
every target sentence was read both with and without prequestions. Prequestions improved
memory only for the prequestioned information, and eye movements showed the same
specificity. Ex-Gaussian models, which separate typical reading time from occasional unusually
long readings, showed that prequestions did not change typical reading of the answer sentences.
Instead, these sentences received more unusually long readings, were looked back to more often,
and were re-read for longer; other sentences were unaffected. Prequestions thus guide attention
selectively rather than heightening it, consistent with additional processing when readers
recognize an answer.

title: Measuring bilingual vocabulary: A systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Alvin Tan, Federica Moro, Gianmatteo Farabolini
abstractRaw: Bilingual vocabulary size is often compared with monolingual scores, especially when bilingual normative data are not available, but there is no agreement on how to measure it. Bilingual scores commonly rely on a single language score, on the total amount of words known across languages (total vocabulary) or on the sum of concepts known in either language (conceptual vocabulary). We conducted a Bayesian network meta-analysis comparing these three bilingual measures against monolingual scores, and analyzed the effect of age, vocabulary domain (receptive and expressive), instrument type (direct or parent-report), language development status and language distance. Out of 3747 records retrieved from ERIC, PubMed, PsycInfo, and Google Scholar, we included 226 studies reporting data on 50,020 children. Conceptual vocabulary did not credibly differ from monolingual scores (g = −0.08, 95% CrI [−0.38, 0.21]), whereas total vocabulary was larger and single-language vocabulary smaller. Across age, total vocabulary moved further from monolingual scores and single-language vocabulary moved closer to them, while conceptual vocabulary showed no reliable change. Bilingual-monolingual differences were more negative for expressive than for receptive vocabulary across bilingual measures, and direct tests widened the gap for single-language scores only. Language development status and language distance had no reliable effects, but both were sparsely sampled. When bilingual vocabulary size has to be compared with the monolingual one, conceptual vocabulary is the closest measure. Evidence remains limited beyond the age of six, in clinical populations and for language pairs that do not include English.
